prompt: Put Shostack's four questions in order.
items: What are we going to do about it?
Did we do a good enough job?

prompt: Match each question to what answering it produces.

pairs.left: What are we going to do about it?
Did we do a good enough job?

prompt: A team spends an hour discussing the portal's security and leaves with no list of threats. What did the hour produce?

choices.text: A threat model, as long as everybody was there
choices.why: Who attended does not replace the list the second question produces.

choices.text: A conversation about security
choices.why: Right. The second question has a concrete output, and without it there is no model.

choices.text: A risk assessment ready for the auditor
choices.why: Risk needs threats to assess first.

choices.text: The first of the four answers, the model
choices.why: The first answer is a drawing of the system, and nothing was drawn.

prompt: Which value statement of the Threat Modeling Manifesto is a warning against reading this course as a list of methods to apply?

choices.text: Doing threat modelling over talking about it
choices.why: That one is about action, not about methods.

choices.text: Continuous refinement over a single delivery
choices.why: That one is about time: the model keeps changing.

choices.text: Finding design issues over checkbox compliance
choices.why: Close, but it is about compliance, not about methods.

choices.text: People and collaboration over processes, methodologies and tools
choices.why: Right. The methods are scaffolding for people who know the system.

prompt: Carla, the security consultant, models the portal alone in a day and hands over sixty threats. What does the lesson expect to be missing?

choices.text: Threats from facts only the builders know
choices.why: Right. Like the reminder worker running with the owner's password: nobody told carla.

choices.text: Nothing, since sixty threats is a complete model
choices.why: A count says nothing about coverage.

choices.text: The generic threats any web application has
choices.why: Those are exactly the ones a specialist alone does find.

choices.text: A risk score for each of the sixty
choices.why: Scores come later (lesson 9); the question is what carla could not see.

prompt: What is the difference between a bug and a flaw?

choices.text: A bug is a small mistake and a flaw is a serious one
choices.why: Either can be serious; the difference is where it was born.

choices.text: A flaw is what a bug becomes once it reaches production
choices.why: Timing does not turn one into the other.

choices.text: A bug departs from the design; a flaw is the design
choices.why: Right. A flaw is implemented faithfully and is still unsafe.

choices.text: A bug is found by people and a flaw by automated tools
choices.why: Roughly the reverse: tools find bugs and walk past flaws.

prompt: Which of these defects at the portal are flaws rather than bugs? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the search joins the patient's text into SQL
choices.why: A bug: the design said parameterised and the code slipped.

choices.text: the webhook trusts any request that says paid
choices.why: A flaw: nobody designed the check.

choices.text: the session cookie was left without HttpOnly
choices.why: A bug in the implementation.

choices.text: the console was designed to answer from the internet
choices.why: A flaw: the design itself exposes it.

prompt: Why does a static analyser have nothing to say about the webhook handler?

choices.text: It was not configured to read webhooks
choices.why: Configuration would not help: there is no dangerous call.

choices.text: The query is parameterised, which hides the problem from the tool
choices.why: The query is fine. It is not what is wrong.

choices.text: The missing signature check leaves no line of code to flag
choices.why: Right. A missing step is invisible to a tool that reads the steps.

choices.text: Static analysis only runs after deployment
choices.why: It runs on the code, before or after; that is not the reason.

prompt: What does the lesson say about the claim that a defect costs a hundred times more in production?

choices.text: Its sources are weak; the mechanism carries the argument
choices.why: Right. What grows is the list of things that have to change.

choices.text: It is a constant measured again by several recent studies
choices.why: The figures trace back to old studies whose data is hard to find.

choices.text: It holds for bugs found in code and not for flaws in design
choices.why: The lesson does not split the claim that way.

choices.text: It applies to large companies only
choices.why: Size is not the problem with the number.

prompt: Which of these are threat modelling? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Asking what can go wrong with a drawing of a new feature
choices.why: Yes: analysis of a representation of the system.

choices.text: Attacking the deployed portal to see what breaks
choices.why: That is a penetration test: evidence about the implementation.

choices.text: Drawing the existing portal and listing its threats
choices.why: Yes. A system that exists can be modelled too.

choices.text: Ticking the controls on a standard checklist
choices.why: A checklist cannot ask what this system needs that is on no list.

prompt: A pentest of the portal finds nothing. What does that say about the webhook flaw?

choices.text: That the flaw is not exploitable from the internet
choices.why: Not finding is not the same as not being there.

choices.text: That the design was right after all
choices.why: The design is unchanged by the test.

choices.text: That a scanner should be run over the portal as well
choices.why: A scanner walks past flaws even more surely.

choices.text: Little: a test covers only what the tester tried
choices.why: Right. A pentest is evidence about what was tried; a model tells it where to look.

prompt: Which of these changes to the portal call for modelling? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a booking field for the health insurance number
choices.why: New personal data: where does it go and who reads it?

choices.text: a new colour on the booking page
choices.why: Nothing about data, trust or entry points changed.

choices.text: letting a partner gym read a patient's bookings
choices.why: Trust changes: a new party with access.

choices.text: replacing the PDF library that reads uploads
choices.why: A dependency that parses untrusted input.

prompt: When does the lesson say a model should be made?

choices.text: Once, at the start of a project
choices.why: That is the phase mistake: the system keeps changing.

choices.text: Whenever the design changes in a way that matters for security
choices.why: Right, as early in that change as it can be drawn.

choices.text: Before every release, whatever changed
choices.why: A colour change does not call for one.

choices.text: After each penetration test
choices.why: The model comes first and tells the test where to look.

prompt: A model of a new field lists every HTTP header of a call the design has not specified yet. What is wrong?

choices.text: It is guessing at an implementation
choices.why: Right. A model is a drawing of a design.

choices.text: Nothing; more detail finds more threats
choices.why: Detail about an implementation that does not exist finds imaginary ones.

choices.text: Headers belong in lesson 3, not here
choices.why: The problem is the level of detail, not the lesson.

choices.text: It should have used a tool instead
choices.why: A tool would not fix modelling something undecided.

prompt: The portal already runs and was never modelled. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Wait for the next redesign, when modelling is cheap
choices.why: Waiting leaves the live flaws where they are.

choices.text: Model it as it is, now
choices.why: Right. It is the most common starting point there is.

choices.text: Run a scanner, since it is too late to model
choices.why: It is not too late, and a scanner misses flaws.

choices.text: Model only the parts written after today
choices.why: The flaws already in production are the urgent ones.

prompt: Where do clinic staff manage the agenda?

choices.text: In the patient portal, with an admin role
choices.why: The console is a separate application.

choices.text: Directly in the records database
choices.why: Nobody edits the database by hand here.

choices.text: In a separate staff console
choices.why: Right: console.vereda.example.

choices.text: In the payment gateway's dashboard
choices.why: The gateway takes money; it holds no agenda.

prompt: Which of the four facts the builders told you is about who may say a payment happened?

choices.text: The worker uses the database owner's password
choices.why: That is about privilege, not payment.

choices.text: The console should only answer the clinics
choices.why: That is about who can reach the console.

choices.text: The database sits in a private network
choices.why: That is about where data is kept.

choices.text: The webhook marks a booking paid when a request says so
choices.why: Right. Nobody checked that the request came from the gateway.

prompt: Why is daniel, who runs the clinics' operations, one of the four people in the examples?

choices.text: daniel wrote most of the original portal code
choices.why: That was ana.

choices.text: The business owns risk acceptance
choices.why: Right. In lesson 12, daniel signs one.

choices.text: daniel is the clinics' security consultant
choices.why: That is carla.

choices.text: daniel manages the cloud account
choices.why: That is bruno.

prompt: How many clinics does Vereda run?
Why is the virtual environment created inside ~/tm?

choices.text: Because pytm only runs from the home directory
choices.why: It runs anywhere the environment is active.

choices.text: To make pip download faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because git requires it
choices.why: git knows nothing about Python environments.

choices.text: To keep pytm out of the system's Python
choices.why: Right. The system's Python is left alone.

prompt: Why is pytm pinned to 1.4.0?

choices.text: Its threat list changes between releases, and lesson 3 quotes a count
choices.why: Right. Another version gives a different number.

choices.text: Later versions do not run on Linux
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: 1.4.0 is the only version on PyPI
choices.why: The failed install listed fifteen.

choices.text: Pinning makes the install faster
choices.why: It changes what is installed, not how fast.

prompt: python3 -c 'import pytm' fails with ModuleNotFoundError right after a working install. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The install silently failed
choices.why: pip said Successfully installed.

choices.text: Python is older than 3.11
choices.why: Then the install would have failed.

choices.text: The shell has no (.venv) active
choices.why: Right. pytm lives only inside the environment.

choices.text: git was not initialised
choices.why: git has nothing to do with importing.

prompt: The command that turns a folder into a git repository whose first branch is main is: git ___ -b main portal-model
Which path does the lesson recommend for the workspace?

choices.text: A virtual machine, whatever computer you have
choices.why: Recommended only where installing is not allowed.

choices.text: An online Codespace
choices.why: It works, and it is the slowest to type in.

choices.text: Your own computer, with WSL on Windows
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the course needs isolating.

choices.text: A server rented for the course
choices.why: Nothing in the course needs one.

prompt: A new feature lets physiotherapists share an exam PDF with a patient's doctor by e-mail link. Which of the four questions does the team answer first?

choices.text: What are we working on?
choices.why: Right: draw the new flow and the new outsider before asking what can go wrong.

choices.text: What can go wrong with e-mail links?
choices.why: That is the second question, and it needs the drawing first.

choices.text: Which control from the checklist covers sharing?
choices.why: A checklist cannot see what this design needs.

choices.text: Did we do a good enough job last time?
choices.why: The review comes after there is something to review.

prompt: Which of these sharing-feature facts are reasons to model it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a party outside Vereda receives health data
choices.why: Trust changes: a new outsider with access.

choices.text: a link that opens a file without signing in
choices.why: A new way in.

choices.text: the share button is green
choices.why: Nothing about data or trust.

choices.text: the feature was requested by daniel
choices.why: Who asked does not change the threats.

prompt: A defect that is a design implemented faithfully, and still unsafe, is a design ___ rather than a bug.
